data.title: Podbranč – Starý hrad, a hillfort at a land gate
data.excerpt: In the distant past the crossings from one land to another were strictly guarded and fortified; such places were known as „land gates“, in Latin portae, through which only a single road led. The hillfort of Podbranč – Starý hrad was built on the lowest rise beside one such crossing, and the circuit of its rampart is more than a kilometre long.
data.metaTitle: Podbranč – Starý hrad, a hillfort at a land gate
data.metaDescription: The hillfort of Podbranč – Starý hrad guarded an important mountain crossing, one of the „land gates“ (portae) through which a single road led.

timeline.title: The earliest occupation (the Eneolithic)

timeline.description: Štefan Janšák was the first to investigate the hillfort, as early as 1913 – it was the first hillfort examined by this important Slovak scholar. It was discovered on 6 August 1913 and examined fairly thoroughly in two days.

timeline.description: The State Archaeological Institute in Martin carried out a trial excavation at the site under the direction of Vojtech Budinský-Krička; the fieldwork was led by Viktor Šemmer.

timeline.description: Viktor Šemmer, together with four workmen, dug four trenches on the terraces and investigated the ramparts of the hillfort with three further trenches.

timeline.title: The demise of the hillfort
timeline.description: After conditions had calmed, the borders had been stabilised and above all after the stone castle had been built on the neighbouring hill, the hillfort lost its significance and came to an end in the 12th century.

children.text:
Even in the distant past the crossings from one land to another were strictly guarded and fortified. The tendency was to keep the number of such crossings as small as possible. As a rule they were formed by places that could be well defended in time of danger (deep valleys, gorges, ravines and the like). Through these, as a rule, only a single road could lead, into which several roads converged before it. Such crossing points formed in the past the „land gates“, in Latin – portae, in Hungarian – kapu, usually – kokapu, a stone gate or stone door. It is understandable that fortified hillforts, and later castles, gradually arose at these crossings.
 
 Podbranč – Starý hrad may well have been such a hillfort, since it was built on the lowest rise beside this crossing (at an elevation of 454 m).

blocks.alt: A lidar image of the hillfort

children.text: Štefan Janšák was the first to investigate the hillfort, as early as 1913. It was in fact the first hillfort that this important Slovak scholar examined. Of the results of his investigation he wrote the following:

„A hillfort of the kind here spoken of we found this summer, on 6 August 1913, not far from the castle of Branč, on the road between Bukovec and the village of Podbranč. There stands a flat hill which the folk call Starý Hrad (the Old Castle). At first we supposed that a castle had originally stood on that spot, similar to Branč, that is to say a medieval structure, and we hoped to find some remains of it; at castles swept entirely from the surface, at least the ground plan is commonly preserved. But we soon convinced ourselves that what we had here was a human habitation of far greater age. In the space of two days we succeeded in examining the hillfort fairly thoroughly, and we also present a picture of it. Our investigations advanced at least so far that we proved with certainty the prehistoric origin of the hillfort.

From the picture every reader may inform himself of the position and the extent of the hillfort. The arrow added in the left-hand corner shows us the direction of north; from it we may determine the other quarters as well. The hillfort is almost egg-shaped and extends lengthwise from east to west. It slopes from north to south, so that it is sheltered from the cold northern winds and, on the contrary, favourably exposed to the effects of the sun’s rays. For life on the hillfort this circumstance was of great importance. The whole hillfort is girdled by an earthwork (a rampart) whose circuit (its entire length) amounts to 1,060 m, that is more than one kilometre. The greatest width of the hillfort amounts to 145 m. The rampart may be clearly made out in all places; nowhere is it disturbed. Only in two places are there entrances leading into the middle of the hillfort. These are on the northern and the eastern side. It is not known whether these entrances were the original ways into the hillfort (for every stronghold had an entrance furnished with a stout gate), or whether people made them later in order to have access to the hill. For a cart road leads through the northern entrance onto the hillfort, along which the peasants drive to the several small fields scattered over the hillfort. The entrance on the eastern side (from the forest) is not used for carts; bushes block it entirely. The north-eastern side of the hillfort is separated from the fields adjoining it by steep rocks, where the peasants quarry stone for building.

blocks.caption: A view of the hillfort from Branč Castle (M. Sladok)
blocks.alt: A view of the hillfort from Branč Castle (M. Sladok)

children.text: Besides the middle earthwork encircling the hillfort, we also found the remains of two further earthworks: an outer one on the southern side (at the very bottom of the picture), and an inner one on the eastern side (on the right in the picture, inside). All around, the earthwork lies above the slope; only at the place marked with the letter c (by the northern exit) does it stand on level ground. For that reason it is at its highest there, and even today, after thousands of years during which it has considerably settled or slipped, it is more than five metres high. On the eastern side, and partly on the north-eastern side of the hillfort, there is dense young woodland; to the north and north-west, beyond the stone quarry, fields (see the picture); to the west sloping pastures; and to the south a stony hillside overgrown with bushes and thorns. In the middle of the hillfort itself lie a few small fields and a pasture.“

At the hillfort Janšák found a number of sherds, a flint tool, bones and several iron finds. Besides that, of course – as later became his good habit – he produced a fine drawing of the ground plan of the hillfort.

As can be seen on Š. Janšák’s ground plan of Starý hrad, the main entrance to the hillfort was on the eastern side, from the direction of Kamenné vráta. The northern entrance, from the direction of Podzámok, was probably built later. Since the inhabitants of the hamlet of Podzámok had small fields on the plateau of the hillfort, they used this northern entrance, which they called the „branka“ (the little gate), as the access road to their fields.

In 1946–1947 the State Archaeological Institute in Martin carried out a trial excavation at the site under the direction of Vojtech Budinský-Krička. The fieldwork was led by Viktor Šemmer, who in 1947, together with four workmen, dug four trenches on the terraces and investigated the ramparts with three further trenches. The finds obtained date the earliest occupation to the Middle Eneolithic (the Channelled Ware culture, named after the way its pottery was decorated), whose bearers liked to seek out and occupy elevated positions and built fortified settlements on them around 2500 BC. Further finds come from the period of the Lusatian culture – the Late Bronze Age to the Early Iron Age. The knoll of the hillfort was occupied again at the time of the Celtic expansion in the Middle and Later La Tène period, and in the Roman period. Occupation then continued, with interruptions, in the Slavic period – in the time of Great Moravia and in the Middle Ages. From the Slavic period come typical
Slavic sherds and a spur with hooks

, dated to the 8th and 9th centuries, that is to the heyday of the Principality of Nitra and subsequently of Great Moravia. The Slavs renewed the hillfort and also improved its defences. The rebuilding of the hillfort by the Slavs in the Great Moravian period was evidently connected with its position above the road which crossed the Lesser Carpathians through the Brezová Pass.

children.text: The hillfort, lying on a promontory, thus consisted of three enclosures and was almost 500 m long. In the second enclosure the foundations of semi-sunken buildings with stone fireplaces in the corner of the rooms were excavated. In the most important part of the hillfort – the acropolis – traces of posts suggest that the timber buildings there may have been more „luxurious“ – built at ground level. Unfortunately, no more detailed excavation has yet been carried out at the hillfort which might bring better insights into its occupation and its inhabitants.

The Slavic occupation of the surrounding country is also attested by the cemeteries in the villages of Hradište pod Vrátnom, in the Podhorie part of Prietrž and in the Majeričky part of the village of Podbranč, not far from Starý hrad, and by the remains of an even older Slavic settlement on the site of the deserted village of Ropov. The hillfort existed even after the fall of Great Moravia. The historian B. Varsik assumes that it was inhabited until the stone castle of Branč was built. After the fall of Great Moravia and a temporary Polish rule, the territory of present-day Slovakia became definitively part of the Hungarian state, which took over the existing system of hillforts from vanished Great Moravia. The hillfort evidently acquired great strategic importance at the time when the territorial interests of the Hungarian and the Bohemian states met. For unlike in the Great Moravian period, Starý hrad now lay on the border of two states, in the zone called the confinium. After conditions had calmed and the borders had been stabilised, and above all after the stone castle had been built on the neighbouring hill, the hillfort lost its significance and came to an end in the 12th century.
